items.title: Policies and procedures
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A policy says what the organisation expects and why; a procedure says how to do it, step by step. Write only what you need: data protection, health and safety, expenses, conduct, complaints. Keep each short and in plain words, name an owner, give a review date, and store them where everyone can find them. A policy nobody has read protects nobody, so tell people about it when they start and when it changes. Check that it works: ask someone to follow the procedure and see where they get stuck. If a rule is never followed, change the rule or change the way you enforce it.

options.text: A policy is for managers only

options.text: Hiding it in a locked drawer

options.text: Ask someone to follow it and see where they get stuck

questions.prompt: If a rule is never followed, what should you do?

options.text: Change the rule or how it is enforced

items.title: Making an annual plan
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: An annual plan turns the strategy into what this year's team will actually do and spend. Start from last year's results and the few goals that matter most, not from a blank sheet. Set a small number of targets that can be measured, name an owner for each, and turn them into a budget: expected income, costs and the cash you will need month by month. Plan for what could go wrong with a sensible reserve, and decide in advance what you will stop doing to make room for new work. Share the plan so everyone can see how their work fits. Review it each quarter and change it when facts change; a plan that is never reviewed is only a wish.

questions.prompt: What is an annual plan for?

options.text: To turn the strategy into what the team will do and spend this year
To replace the need for a budget

questions.prompt: Why name an owner for each target?

options.text: So the owner can take the credit
So someone is responsible for making it happen

questions.prompt: What should an annual plan decide in advance?

options.text: Which targets to hide from staff
What you will stop doing to make room for new work

questions.prompt: A plan that is never reviewed during the year is best described as:

options.text: A wish rather than a plan

items.title: Running a strategic review
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A strategic review steps back from daily work to ask whether the business is heading the right way. Look at what has changed: customers, competitors, costs, technology and rules. Compare results with the goals, and ask honestly what is working, what is not and what you would not start today. Check the strengths you rely on and the risks you have been ignoring. Then choose a few priorities for the next phase and, just as important, decide what to drop. Write the conclusions and the reasons, share them, and set a date to check progress. A review that only confirms the current plan has probably not asked hard enough questions.

questions.prompt: What is a strategic review?

options.text: A review of staff holiday records
A step back to ask whether the business is heading the right way

questions.prompt: Which question belongs in a strategic review?

options.text: Who is responsible for the office plants?
What was on the menu last Tuesday?
What would we not start today if we were beginning again?
How many emails were sent today?

questions.prompt: Why decide what to drop, as well as what to start?

options.text: Starting new work is not allowed
Time and money are limited, so new priorities need room

questions.prompt: A review that always confirms the current plan most likely means:

options.text: The hard questions were not asked
Nobody needs to review it again

items.title: Succession planning
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Succession planning prepares for the day someone key leaves, whether planned or sudden. Start by listing the roles the business cannot do without, including the owner's. For each, note what knowledge and relationships sit with one person and write them down. Identify who could step in, now or with development, and plan their training. Keep access details and key contacts where a trusted person can reach them. For an owner who wants to hand over or sell, start years ahead: build a business that runs without them and prepare the people who will take over. Review the plan every year.

options.text: Preparing for the day a key person leaves

questions.prompt: Which roles should you list first?

options.text: The roles the business cannot do without

questions.prompt: Why write down what only one person knows?

options.text: So the business does not depend on that person's memory

questions.prompt: An owner wants to sell in five years. When should preparation start?

options.text: On the day of the sale

items.title: Advisers and mentors
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A good adviser or mentor sees what you cannot and tells you what you do not want to hear. Decide what you need: general guidance, specific skills such as law or accounting, or someone who has built a similar business. Look for people with relevant experience who will be honest, not only friendly. Be clear about what you want from them and how much time you are asking for. Prepare questions, listen, and then act on what you decide is right. Thank them and report what happened. Pay professional advisers fairly and check their qualifications. Use more than one voice on big decisions.

options.text: It makes the time useful for both of you

options.text: Decide what is right for you and act, then report back

items.title: Controls and approvals
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Controls protect the business from mistakes and fraud without strangling it. Set clear limits for who can approve spending, signing contracts and paying people, with higher amounts needing more than one person. Separate duties so the person who orders is not the person who pays. Keep simple records of each approval. Review a sample of transactions regularly and reconcile bank accounts. Make rules proportionate: too many slow the work and invite workarounds, too few leave you exposed. Explain the reasons, and apply the same rules to the owner.

Why separate who orders from who pays?

options.text: So one person cannot misuse the process alone

options.text: Work slows and people find ways around them

questions.prompt: Why should the owner follow the same rules?

options.text: Rules that exempt the boss lose credibility and protection

items.title: Lessons learned
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A lessons-learned review turns experience into improvement. Hold it soon after a project, event or failure, with the people who were there, in a spirit of learning, not blame. Ask four things: what did we plan, what happened, why was there a difference, and what will we do differently. Look for causes in the process, not just in individuals. Write down a few clear actions with owners and dates, and share them with people who will face similar situations. Check later that the actions were done. Lessons that sit in a file and change nothing are not lessons.

options.text: Soon after the project or event, with the people involved
With people who were not there

questions.prompt: Which question belongs in a lessons-learned review?

options.text: What will we do differently next time?

questions.prompt: Why look for causes in the process, not just individuals?

options.text: Fixing the process stops the same problem recurring

questions.prompt: What makes a lesson real?

options.text: An action with an owner and date that is then done

items.body: People who start a business together, as partners, friends or family, often avoid awkward conversations that later cause the biggest fights. Agree early, in writing: who owns what share, who does what, how decisions are made, how each is paid, what happens if one wants to leave, dies, becomes ill or stops contributing, and how disputes are settled. For a company, a shareholders' agreement can cover this; for a partnership, a partnership agreement. Revisit it as roles change. Family ties make clear agreements more important, not less. Take legal advice.

questions.prompt: Why agree terms in writing between co-founders?

options.text: To avoid disputes later about shares, roles and leaving
It is only for large companies

questions.prompt: Which should a co-founder agreement cover?

options.text: Who owns what, who does what and what happens if someone leaves

questions.prompt: Which agreement can cover this for a company?
Why are written agreements important in a family business?

options.text: Close ties make clear agreements more important, not less
